lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion in the Solar System
top_level_objectives: Observe Mars’s apparent retrograde motion from Earth’s perspective and describe the pattern over time.
Explain retrograde motion as an apparent effect caused by the relative motion of Earth and Mars in a heliocentric model.
Compare Mars’s retrograde motion with that of Jupiter and Saturn and relate the differences to orbital distance and speed.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the observational puzzle of retrograde motion and establish what students will track in the sky over several weeks.
key_visuals: A dark sky dome with constellation background and a labeled path showing Mars drifting among the stars
A simple time slider or calendar cue indicating nights passing
Highlighted positions of Mars forming a small loop in the sky
student_actions: Observe Mars’s changing position against the background stars
Advance time through several nights and notice the eastward drift slow, reverse, and resume
Record the overall shape of Mars’s path

scenes.brief_purpose: Focus attention on the timing and shape of Mars’s apparent loop so students can identify the retrograde phase precisely.
key_visuals: A zoomed-in view of the same star field with Mars positions marked night by night
Directional arrows showing eastward and westward motion
Labels indicating the start, middle, and end of the retrograde interval
student_actions: Track the sequence of Mars positions across the loop
Identify when Mars appears to stop and move backward
Compare the retrograde segment with the longer prograde motion before and after it

scenes.brief_purpose: Prompt students to think about what kind of model might explain the observed loop before revealing the heliocentric cause.
key_visuals: A simplified comparison between an Earth-centered-looking sky view and a basic solar system diagram
A visual cue suggesting an old-style explanatory model with extra circles or paths
A question prompt centered on why a planet would appear to reverse direction
student_actions: Consider how the loop might be explained from an Earth-centered perspective
Predict what moving planets might need to do to create the observed pattern
Test their intuition against the observed sky motion

scenes.brief_purpose: Reveal the heliocentric explanation by showing Earth and Mars moving in their orbits from an external viewpoint.
key_visuals: A Sun-centered view with Earth on a smaller, faster orbit and Mars on a larger, slower orbit
Both planets moving smoothly in the same direction around the Sun
A line of sight from Earth to Mars changing as Earth approaches and passes Mars
student_actions: Watch Earth overtake Mars and connect that event to the apparent backward motion
Relate the changing line of sight to the loop seen from Earth
Explain in their own words why the motion appears retrograde

scenes.brief_purpose: Use a familiar everyday analogy to reinforce that the retrograde effect is caused by relative motion, not Mars actually reversing its orbit.
key_visuals: A roadway or lane analogy with one vehicle passing another more slowly moving vehicle
A mirrored pairing between the car example and the Earth-Mars orbital view
Simple arrows emphasizing the faster inner path overtaking the slower outer path
student_actions: Compare the car-passing analogy to the planet diagram
Identify which object is the moving observer and which is being overtaken
State the key idea that apparent backward motion can result from motion in the observer’s frame

scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the concept by showing that Jupiter and Saturn also exhibit retrograde motion, but with smaller loops because of their more distant orbits.
key_visuals: A side-by-side comparison of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn paths over time
Smaller, subtler loops for Jupiter and Saturn relative to Mars
Orbital distance cues showing increasing separation from the Sun
student_actions: Compare the size and frequency of retrograde loops among the outer planets
Infer how orbital distance affects the strength of the relative-motion effect
Summarize why Mars’s retrograde motion is easier to notice than Jupiter’s or Saturn’s
